l: this world, Sohila (Kirtan Sohila)
s: This world is involved in wickedness and superstition; those who know God are saved from it.

l: the next world, Sohila (Kirtan Sohila)
s: provides happiness The next world is described as a place where those who earn God's name will abide in happiness.

l: Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Asa ki War (Asa di Var), translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe in The Sikh Religion (1909), is a devotional and moral composition containing pauris and sloks attributed chiefly to Guru Nanak and Guru Angad, with Guru Har Gobind named. It begins by affirming one true, self-existent, fearless, beneficent Creator and repeatedly presents the Guru as essential: without the Guru, neither vast light, learning, ritual, nor outward religious practice can dispel spiritual darkness or bring salvation. Across its sequence, the work describes God as creator, sustainer, judge, and ruler of every world, creature, action, life, death, and destiny. God records deeds, appoints Dharmraj for judgment, separates the truthful from those attached to mammon, and alone remains fearless, true, and permanent amid a passing world. Human beings die, become ashes, face the account of their acts, and may undergo transmigration; grace, the divine Name, truth, humility, love, and the Guru’s instruction provide the way through this condition. The text persistently rejects pride, greed, falsehood, hypocrisy, caste pretension, dishonest earnings, ritual purity, purchased religious marks, pilgrimages, austerity, and merely verbal or external devotion. It contrasts them with inward purity, honest work, mercy, contentment, continence, charity, service, supplication, and remembrance of God. Its spiritual janeu is mercy, contentment, continence, and truth rather than a cotton thread; true impurity lies in greed, falsehood, coveting, slander, superstition, and attachment. The later portions deepen its ethical warning: worldly beauty, authority, possessions, relationships, and religious display cannot survive death, while people must bear their own deeds. The faithful servant effaces himself and follows the master’s will; one who competes with the master loses honour. The work concludes by returning to God’s comprehensive power: God creates, orders, fills, sustains, regenerates, and governs all beings, while His greatness is beyond expression and He alone is the abiding Place.

l: Asa ki War (Asa di Var), Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: A War translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe, presented in The Sikh Religion volume 1 and including sloks.

l: God, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: God is the one true, formless, fearless, immortal, unborn, self-existent Creator: great, beneficent, unrivalled, omnipotent, and the Lord of all gods and souls. God creates the world, different worlds, animals, people, lands, waters, Maya, vessels, and all creation; gives names, life, sustenance, duties, and gifts, while also ordaining birth and death, destroying creation again, judging acts, and causing people to act. God knows all things, human utterances and feelings, and the condition of animals; sees all, pervades animate and inanimate creation, and takes thought and care for the world and its creatures. God's court, order, command, power, justice, glory, and divine acts are true, with an imperishable court and immovable seat. God acts by His own will and cannot be commanded. He looks with favour on some, gives grace, greatness, truth, divine knowledge, and regeneration, blending some beings with Himself; others are led astray and wander through births. God may be known through the Guru and divine instruction, dwells in the heart of the truly pure, and is sought through remembrance, devotion, praise, supplication, and freedom from pride. The account moves from God's essential nature, through creation and governance of all beings, to judgement, favour, knowledge, and the destiny of those who receive or lack God's grace.

l: Guru Har Gobind, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Guru Har Gobind is named in the unit.

l: sloks, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Sloks in Asa ki War, written by the first Guru, are sung to the air of Tunda As Raja.

l: Guru Nanak, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Guru Nanak is presented as a speaker, teacher, Guru, Commander, and devoted slave of the bright God. Across the records, he teaches that God alone is true, unrivalled, all-powerful, formless, independent, and the maker, ruler, and caretaker of the world. God knows what humans do not, including whether burning or burial is better, ordains regard for people according to their regard for God, gives differing conditions, and causes beings to act. Guru Nanak repeatedly contrasts this divine truth with a world marked by falsehood, pride, corruption, suffering, death, transmigration, and the consequences of deeds. His central teaching is that the true Guru, divine grace, God's name, meditation on the True One, love, devotion, humility, mercy, charity, and divine knowledge lead people toward truth, comfort, honour, purity, and salvation. Without the Guru and grace, even extensive good works, study, bravery, charity, penance, reading, ritual, and outward religious marks are of no avail. He rejects hypocrisy, violence, greed, falsehood, slander, empty observance, arguments, worship of stones, and external purity, insisting instead on God in the heart and inner purity. The account unfolds through praise of God's true order and power, then warnings about the fearful, changing, and false world. It develops a sustained critique of corrupt rulers, priests, pretenders, caste, ritual practice, and the purchased janeu, replacing them with a true discipline of mercy, contentment, continence, truth, and praise of the Name. It ends by affirming longing for God, the gift received when the Lord is pleased, the servant's love for the master, and God's continuing power to make, fill, regenerate, and sustain all beings.

l: Guru Angad, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Guru Angad is presented as a teacher of the Guru’s instruction and of devotion to God. His teachings begin by portraying the Guru as essential light against profound darkness. They describe the world as the True One’s dwelling, governed by God’s order, which frees some from mammon and reveals God to the holy. He elevates repetition of the one God’s name above social and religious duties, and defines true love as absorption in God rather than worldly attachment. He further teaches service, humility, truthful speech, friendship, praise of God, and respect for God’s works. He concludes by affirming God’s ordering of creation, including animals’ birth and death.

l: True Guru, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: True Guru is a true Guru, the greatest benefactor and giver of life to the world. He transforms men into demigods without delay and is necessary to dispel spiritual darkness, find the way, awaken those asleep in ignorance, and gain divine knowledge. Obtained by God’s grace when the Kind One looks with kindness, he communicates the Word to the soul after many births, gives divine instruction, removes pride, preaches the Truest of the true, and fixes God’s name and praises in the heart. God is within the true Guru and manifests and reveals Himself through the Guru’s favour; without the true Guru, none has found God. With truth in his heart and worldly love banished from within him, the Guru leads people to God, salvation, comfort, and truth. He is a merciful boat that saves those who recognize him as such. Possessing all greatness, he can cause people to meet God and behold His greatness; when pleased, he removes evil from within and causes God’s praises to dwell in the heart. When God is pleased, the nine treasures are obtained.

l: world, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: The world is God’s creation: made, named, cared for, empowered, and observed by God. It is great as God’s world, yet a temporary human residence and a stage of entanglements. God decreed transmigration within it, while its rulers, subjects, dwellings, possessions, relationships, beauty, sweetness, and wealth are described as false. Burdened in fear, the world passes away: whatever comes into it eventually departs, and every person’s turn arrives.

l: Maya, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Maya was created by God through His power.

l: men, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: The records portray men as mortal, morally accountable beings whose lives are often ruled by pride, ignorance, desire, and attachment to worldly pleasure. A man may enjoy himself, gain wealth or greatness, live in mansions and palaces, display wealth, exercise authority, and fix his heart on horses and women, yet he forgets death and ultimately becomes ashes. Death takes even the great and wealthy; afterward comes judgment, an account of acts, suffering for one’s own acts, and no shelter for the condemned. Pride makes men true or false, leads them toward hell or heaven, blinds them, and leaves them without deliverance or salvation. Religious exertions, pilgrimages, garbs, fasting, silence, hardship, or dwelling in wilderness and cremation-grounds do not by themselves remove this burden. Some men do not know their origin and hold excessive opinions of themselves; in the blackness of the age they lack divine knowledge and may become demons. Yet the course can change: desire for and abiding in truth, meeting the true Guru, fixing God’s name in the heart, being favoured by God, and destroying pride through the Word bring freedom from hopes and fears and reveal God’s gate.

l: life, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Life in water can be wasted by man, ending in ashes and judgment when he remains blind to his condition.

l: Dharmraj, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Dharmraj, appointed by God, sits fearfully at God's gate and judges and records animals' acts.

l: creation, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Creation exists by God's power: God creates, pervades, and commands the nether regions, heavens, earth, and all creatures.

l: account of his acts, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Man’s acts are read before the Judge to pass sentence, and he must bear their results despite outward austerities or unusual practices.

l: divine order, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: God's order governs the world, determines people’s spiritual fate regarding mammon, and guides worshippers; obeying it makes a person acceptable and leads toward God's court.

l: God's court, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: adjudges judgment of acts [according to real truth] God's court is described as true. At His own court, the real truth is adjudged, and those attached to mammon are separated and removed.

l: divine power, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Divine power produces creation, sacred books, human qualities and the elements; it causes seeing, hearing, fear, happiness and affection, so everything exists by it.

l: meditation on the True One, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Meditation on the True One is practised by the truthful and devotees, who Guru Nanak declares true; the speaker begs from them, valuing devotion over high caste.

l: birth and death, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: is_a falsehood [the falsest of the false] Those who are born and die are described by Guru Nanak as the falsest of the false.

l: divine glory, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: God's glory is called great because His name is great, His justice is true, His seat is immovable, He understands utterances, knows feelings, gives without consulting others, and is all in all Himself. His acts cannot be described.

l: divine will, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: All that God did and has to do depends on His own will.

l: God's court, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: God's court is the True One's chamber and dwelling, seen when pride is removed. It judges both literate people and illiterate saints hereafter. Those who obey the Master's order reach it, receive the heart's desired fruit, wear honour, and enter through the true spiritual thread.

l: mammon, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Mammon abides in the world as God’s chamber, fosters pride and pain in the heart, and separates those attached from the divine court.

l: holiness, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: is_known_as holy [the state of one to whom God reveals Himself] The person to whom God reveals Himself is known as holy.

l: animals, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Animals are created beings in all creation, living in water, dry land, and fourteen worlds. God records their names, creates their many species, forms, colours, genera, and kinds, cares for them, knows their condition, and appoints Dharmraj to judge their acts. They have no power of their own; all unfolds by God's power.

l: names, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: are_recorded animals [by God] God recorded the names of the animals He created.

l: judgment of acts, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: is_conducted_by Dharmraj God appointed Dharmraj to judge and record acts. At God's court, the real truth is adjudged.

l: hell, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Hell receives deceivers and the false with blackened faces, and naked people; it appears very formidable to a naked man.

l: Word, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: is_communicated_by true Guru [to the soul] The true Guru communicates the Word to the soul after it has wandered through many births.

l: Veds, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: The four Veds are religious compositions, described by Hindus as true, yet their study reveals four different doctrines and teachings about the Lord, God's name, truth, and the Kal age; they are insufficient for salvation.

l: the true Name, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: The true Name is the Formless divine. Repeating it prevents hell, while saints praise God through it and remain in everlasting joy. It gives sacrificial marks and threads their value, and adoration and praise provide honour and a true thread. From beginning to end, it is presented as essential to repetition, worship, sacrifice, and speech while eating.

l: soul, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: The soul belongs to God and is known by one who knows its secrets. After man becomes ashes, it passes away; at death it departs without the external janeu, while receiving one of mercy, contentment, continence, and truth.

l: Death, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Death is ordained and takes every man after life regardless of greatness or wealth; men forget it amid women’s chambers, authority, and pleasure until old age comes and youth fails.

l: ministers of Death, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Ministers of Death serve Death, chain and take people away for judgment, and devour those devoid of divine knowledge.

l: Judge, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: The Judge sits on a seat, reads the account of a man's acts, and passes sentence.

l: fear, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Fear governs bodies, natural forces, divine beings, mighty men, and people’s coming and going; God, the Formless One, alone is without it.

l: divine knowledge, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Divine knowledge is the highest duty: difficult to seek or speak of, gained by God’s grace rather than words, skill, or orders. Without it, people are consumed by the minister of death. It requires a guru, restrains the mind, and washes away impurity.

l: God's grace, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: gives divine knowledge [to man] God's grace enables a person to obtain divine knowledge.

l: pride, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Pride is a chronic disease and trammel that affects birth, death, actions, thoughts, status, knowledge, wealth, and spiritual condition, causing repeated transmigration. Though people practise it despite the world's impermanence, it is linked to senseless discussion and excessive self-opinion, and is removed through Guru, God's grace, the Word, devotion, and medicine in the heart.

l: food, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Food is made holy when ghi is added to holy corn, water, fire, and salt, then becomes impure upon entering a sinful body.

l: people who have meditated on God, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: A group who meditate on God as the truest of the true. They perform real worship, become contented, reject evil, do good and honest deeds, live on little, break worldly entanglements, and ultimately find God.

l: Guru's instruction, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: gives knowledge [to disciples] Through the Guru's instruction, disciples obtain knowledge that the Kind One saves those upon whom He looks with favor.

l: the Kind One, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: saves those on whom he looketh with favour [with favour] The Kind One saves those upon whom He looks with favor.

l: entanglements of the world, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Entanglements bind beings to worldly stage properties and vessels, swinging them by their acts; dancers and laughers ultimately weep when they depart.

l: fear of God, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Fear of God is a disposition in hearts, unfolding as love in those who possess it.

l: love, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Love is found with fear of God and leads to salvation through devotion and lowliness. It moves good people to weep, laugh, or be silent, and makes them care only for the true Master. Worldly attachment is rejected; true love remains absorbed in God, as a servant in the master.

l: good deeds, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Good deeds bring benefit when pursued with humility; those seeking advantage are instructed to act well and remain lowly.

l: death, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Death, disguised as old age, arrives despite efforts to stave it off and ends all remaining when one’s measure is full.

l: Musalmans, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Musalmans praise and study Shariat, while God’s servants serve Him to behold Him; their ashes become burning, weeping vessels and bricks.

l: Hindus, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Hindus praise the incomparable Praised One, affirm four Veds, bathe in holy streams, worship idols, and use copious sandal incense.

l: Jogis, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Jogis meditate on God the Creator, call God the Unseen and Bright One, and seek divine knowledge.

l: saints, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Saints hunger to praise God, live in everlasting joy day and night, please God's heart, adorn God's gate, and hymn God's praises. The text seeks the dust of their feet, while those outside God's favour cannot enter and wander through many births.

l: salvation, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Salvation is obtained through meeting the true Guru and through love, devotion, humility, and repeating God's name. Pretended religious people, though seeking its door, spoil their acts and do not know the way. It unfolds from the Guru’s example to warnings, then stated means.

l: transmigration, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Transmigration is repeated wandering caused by pride, shaped by previous acts, and decreed by the Creator who made the world.

l: worship, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: leads_to happiness [when directed toward the Lord] Worship of the Lord is presented as a way to find happiness. The text urges remembrance of the Lord through worship.

l: man's evil, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: is_known known [to the True One] Man's evil becomes known, and the True One sees all.

l: grace, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: has_mark true Grace provides the true mark. Without the mark of grace, numerous good acts, charities, penances, acts of bravery, studies, and readings are of no avail.

l: truth, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Truth dwells in the true Guru’s heart, is received from the true Lord through meeting the Guru, and makes a person true when held in the heart. It is medicine for all, removing sin, and is possessed by saints. Truth is in dearth during the age, though it was desired and lived in the Sat age and was the driver in front in the Dwapar age.

l: the fool, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: A fool does not know truth, wastes life through obstinacy, acts by his own understanding, and makes friendship unprofitable; he may do one or two things well but spoils the rest.

l: books, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Books can fill carts, boats, pits, and lifetimes of reading, yet the text says one word, God's name, outweighs them all.

l: God's name, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: God's name is the only word that truly counts, the highest duty for all, and is everywhere, like the sun in heaven. Meeting the true Guru fixes it in the heart, bringing comfort, freedom from hopes and fears, and an abiding place. Those who sow its seed depart with honour. Repeating it removes sins and leads to salvation; in the Kal age it was called Allah.

l: caste, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Caste is presented as people’s claim to high or low status, contrasted with devotion to God; the speaker identifies as low caste, and caste has no power in the next world’s new order.

l: man, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Man is false when falsehood is in him: he loves falsehood and forgets God. With truth in his heart, he is known as true, loves God, knows the true way, receives true instruction, shows mercy, and performs charity. He inquires of the true Guru, then rests in his own heart. By obeying God’s order and serving the Master, he becomes acceptable to the Lord, reaches God’s court, gains his heart’s desire and a robe of honour, and attains salvation through enraptured hearing of the Name.

l: falsehood, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Falsehood makes false man love falsehood and forget the Creator; it is tied to covetousness, impurity of the tongue, and dwells in the false one’s mouth. Prevailing in this age as master of the mint, it brings contempt, but cleansing and devotion remove it and wash away sin.

l: friendship, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: with fool [not profitable] Friendship with a fool is unprofitable. Friendship for a fool and love for a great man are compared to lines drawn on water, leaving neither trace nor mark.

l: sin, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: is_village_accountant village accountant Sin is described with greed as ruler and village accountant in the corrupt age.

l: service, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: can_ruin man [when scant] Service should be performed with humility and without pride, quarrelsomeness, or excessive talk. Faithful service according to the master's wishes brings honour and double wages.

l: seed of the Name, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: The seed of the Name, sown whole, germinates in the proper season; a half-seed cannot germinate.

l: devotion, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Devotion dyes the body through fear and modesty, removes falsehood, and leads to salvation with love and lowliness.

l: greed, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Greed rules as sin and heart impurity, driving bribes, deceit, and fools’ accumulation of wealth.

l: lust, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Lust is a minister who summons, examines, and judges people.

l: worldly pleasure, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Worldly pleasure is a disease that excludes desire for God wherever it exists.

l: Brahmans, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Brahmans are a group said to have a duty to read Veds, sound shells, perform Hindu worship, and enjoy viands. They bear sacrificial marks, reddish dhotis, blue clothes, and knives. The records condemn their capital, dealings, maintenance, bodies, actions, and hearts as false or defiled, calling them the world’s butchers. They take bread from malechhas, eat he-goats, and tightly exclude others from cooking squares while performing ablutions after meals.

l: vessel, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: A vessel is necessary for everyone’s existence, involved from conception and birth through marriage, friendship, and worldly passage. It gives birth to kings; when one vessel dies, another is sought, continuing the vessel’s cycle.

l: Kal age, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Kal age is an age where passion carries falsehood; Atharv belongs to it, Allah is named, blue clothes are worn, and Turks and Pathans rule.

l: Lord, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: The Lord is a compassionate, merciful true Master who created the world, infused it with power, owns life and soul, beholds its changes, and judges the wicked. Good people love, contemplate, and obey Him; through His compassion, worshippers abide by His order and do His work, while those attached to mammon are wrecked.

l: simmal-tree of the desert, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: The simmal-tree of the desert is very tall and thick, yet birds approach hopefully and leave disappointed by its insipid fruit, unwholesome flowers, and useless leaves.

l: wicked man, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: The wicked man repeatedly bows, but his impure heart makes all his bowing of no avail.

l: vain religion, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: is_a religion [verily vain] The vain religion consists of outward practices such as reading books, performing twilight devotions, arguing, worshipping stones, sitting like cranes, uttering falsehoods, meditating on the Gayatri, and wearing religious marks and garments. Guru Nanak says that without the true Guru, this religion does not provide the way.

l: good and bad deeds, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: yield fruit [the fruit obtained by man] A person obtains the fruit of the good or bad deeds that person has done. Sovereignty and worldly success do not prevent the person from proceeding by the narrow road.

l: sins, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: are_regretted by man [after being committed] A person will regret the sins committed after leaving earthly raiment and pleasing beauty behind and facing what follows.

l: Slok XV, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: is_a slok Slok XV teaches that mercy, contentment, continence, and truth form a lasting janeu for the soul. It contrasts this spiritual thread with the external cotton janeu and describes its failure at death.

l: Pauri XV, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: is_a pauri Pauri XV teaches that a person whom the Lord treats compassionately will do the Master's work and worship according to God's order. Such a person reaches God's court, receives the fruit desired by the heart, and is clothed with a robe of honour.

l: the Brahman, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: The Brahman is a guru of the Hindus. He buys and wears a cotton janeu, declares his role, twists and places neck strings on others, accepts hire for marriages, and reads fate papers. He purifies himself, receives untouched food, and eats while reading Sanskrit verses.

l: janeu, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Janeu is described as two threads: a spiritual thread for the soul, made from mercy, contentment, continence, and truth, and a purchased cotton ritual thread. The cotton thread costs four damris, is worn by a Brahman around a man’s neck, grows old, is discarded and replaced, and falls at death. The lasting spiritual janeu remains intact, clean, unburned, and present, qualifying one for entry into God’s court.

l: adorned women, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: are adorned with every aid to beauty Adorned women are among the pleasures and displays on which men fix their hearts. Men behold their women’s chambers and forget death.

l: Muhammadans, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: accept Brahmans [in their court] Muhammadans are associated with by those who publicly read the Quran while performing Hindu worship at home. Their court accepts people wearing blue clothes, and those people take bread from malechhas while worshipping the Purans.

l: malechhas, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Malechhas provide bread that some people eat while maintaining Hindu ritual practices. The text also describes people as taking bread from malechhas while seeking acceptance in the Muhammadans' court.

l: ancestors, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Ancestors receive a robber’s offering and, in the next world, are made out to be thieves.

l: impurity, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Impurity is present in everything physically, yet its deeper forms are greed, falsehood, wrongful gazing, slander, superstition, and attachment to worldly things.

l: acts and accountability, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Every person must bear the results of their own acts and adjust their own account.

l: evil person, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: The evil person is foolish, inwardly foul yet outwardly fair, evil in mind, body, and reputation, rejected in God's court, spat upon, and punished with shoe-beatings.

l: good people, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Good people may wear rags outwardly and silk within, love and remain in God’s love, care exclusively for the true Master, beg at God’s door, and eat only what God gives.

l: evil deeds, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: cause suffering [for the person who commits them] Evil deeds bring suffering. The text instructs a person to do absolutely nothing evil and to look well before acting.

l: servant, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: A servant performs service and is defined as absorbed in love of the master. Pride, quarrelsomeness, and excessive talk prevent pleasing the master. By effacing himself and serving, he obtains honour; by following the master’s wishes, he receives greater honour and double wages. Vying with the master instead brings jealousy, loss of a large salary, and shoe-beating on the mouth.

l: master, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: The master is displeased by a proud, quarrelsome, and talkative servant. A servant who vies with the master excites his jealousy, loses his large salary, and receives shoe-beating on the mouth.

l: longing for God, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: is_acceptable_to God Longing for God leads the person who has it to meet Him. Nanak says that this longing is acceptable.

l: praising God, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: gives pleasure Praising God is associated with pleasure. Nanak says that pleasure is found in praising God.

l: man, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: Man’s heart is revealed in speech, making lip-worship futile. He cannot sow poison and expect ambrosia, must perform God-destined work, lives by God’s gifts, and has God alone as his abiding place.

l: Slok XXII, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: has_author Guru Angad Slok XXII contains teachings attributed to Guru Angad about humble service, the revelation of the heart, the futility of friendship with a fool, falsehood, supplication to God, and praising God.

l: Pauri XXII, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: has_author Guru Angad Pauri XXII teaches that a servant who acts according to the master's wishes receives honour and double wages. It warns that competing with the master brings jealousy, loss of salary, and shoe-beating, and concludes that God must be implored rather than commanded.

l: gift, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: A gift obtained by personal asking is contrasted with the wonderful gift received when God is pleased.

l: service, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: has fear [fear of the master does not depart] Service in which the fear of the master does not depart is contrasted with service marked by absorption in the love of the master.

l: destruction, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: God Himself again destroys.

l: people (those with chains or horses), Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: A group includes people with neck chains and others riding many horses; God causes them to act.

l: care, Asa ki War (Asa di Var)
s: is_for world The one who made the world takes care of it.

l: Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: This document is a sequence of devotional teachings attributed repeatedly to Nanak, arranged across many Rags, Wars, Ashtapadis, Chhants, and related units. Its central concern is the human path to God: God alone is true, eternal, creating, sustaining, judging, forgiving, and present in all creatures; the Guru, the Word, and remembrance of God’s Name enable people to know and unite with Him. From the opening Sri Rag onward, the text contrasts happiness, honour, purity, truth, virtue, love, and deliverance with pride, mammon, attachment, greed, counterfeit conduct, and worldly wealth. Human bodies, youth, beauty, status, possessions, and family ties are transient; death, destiny, judgment, suffering, and transmigration confront all. The true Guru’s instruction, Sat Sangat, obedience to God’s will, truthful conduct, humility, contentment, mercy, service, good deeds, and devotion to the Name lead toward God’s court, peace, and salvation. A recurring figure is the longing woman or bride, separated from her Beloved and dishonoured until she seeks Him through love, virtue, the Name, and divine favour. Her fulfillment represents union with God. Nanak also presents himself as God’s servant and minstrel, receiving the true Name, praising the Indescribable, and acknowledging his own foolishness and dependence on his Master. Throughout, the units reject empty outward religion: ritual washing, alms, pilgrimage, austerity, religious dress, ceremonies, learning, yogic practices, external observances, caste, status, and displays of piety are futile when they lack God’s Name, the Word, and the Guru’s guidance. Particular criticism is directed at hypocrisy among Jogis, Qazis, Brahmans, Musalmans, Pandits, gurus, pirs, and idol worshippers; Bihagre ki War questions worship of stones that themselves sink. The document closes in Prabhati by reaffirming the same conclusion: religious acts without knowledge of God are futile, while those imbued with the Word, guided by the true Guru, and devoted to the Name overcome desire, pride, false wisdom, defilement, strife, and separation from the True One.

l: Sri Rag, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a hymn Sri Rag teaches that man should reject intoxicating illusion, counterfeit conduct, pride, and attachment to worldly adornments. It directs man toward truth, virtue, God's name, the Guru, and service to God as the means of happiness and honour in God's court.

l: Ashtapadi, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a hymn Ashtapadi praises God's greatness and teaches that all are wives of the Spouse who must seek genuine love rather than hypocrisy. It explains that the Guru, the Word, God's name, truth, and love deliver man from pride, ritualism, worldly attachment, and the ocean of the world.

l: Nanak, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Nanak is a human being, teacher, minstrel, devotee, and speaker of compositions whose life and teaching center on God, the true Guru, the Word, and God’s Name. He begins as an out-of-work minstrel, then serves by singing the Word, praising God, teaching divine knowledge, and seeking truth through searching, observation, and God. He seeks the pure love and nectar of the Name as the wealth, capital, and necklace of his heart, takes shelter in it, and asks for no other gift. He portrays himself humbly as blind, foolish, a slave of slaves, God’s slave, a dog of God’s court, and one sacrificed ever to God. Though he says he performs no service, he bears his Master’s name, thinks exclusively of God, receives understanding from God, makes his heart a temple, and is not born again because the one word dwells there. His teachings reject pride, worldly wealth, status, ritual, external cleansing, hypocrisy, empty display, bodily life, and attachment without God’s Name. He teaches that the Guru, Name, devotion, humility, truth, contentment, good works, love, and remembrance lead to happiness, honour, deliverance, and union with God; sin, pride, and turning away from God bring suffering. He drinks God’s elixir, remains absorbed in God, and declares that the pious who remain so are perennial. He ends by teaching that the true Guru unites man with God, ending sorrow, sin, and death.

l: God, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: God is the one, true, eternal Giver, Creator, Lord, Benefactor, and support of the soul. Immortal, imperishable, invisible, inscrutable, endless, unborn, and without partner, God owns life and the soul, has full storehouses in every age, and possesses all knowledge as Commander. God creates, sustains, destroys, and reanimates the three worlds and all things without consultation; restrains sea and land; causes the world’s garden to flourish; and gives, controls, or removes human power. God grants each human term of life according to past acts, dispenses weal and woe, gives countlessly, and causes all things to happen. God pervades everything through love: the three worlds, every heart, creatures in water, dry land, nether regions, and firmament. Near the heart and dwelling there as King, Emperor, and Dispenser, God is also figured as Relisher, Enjoyer, fisherman, fish, water, net, and bait. God looks on all things with favour, guards human beings day and night, cares for and protects Nanak, and may favour, test, pardon, transform, or separate people as God pleases. God can change a raven into a swan, while the perfect obtain sight and the fool finds no place. The central response is love, God’s name, service, the Guru’s instruction, protection, and the favouring glance. God gives understanding and knowledge, is known through God’s word, and is found through love. True love preserves the devotee in honour; seeking God brings peace, happiness, truth, emancipation, and deliverance. After emancipation, God blends with man. God’s court may be seen in one’s own home under the Guru’s instruction. The records also describe God as forgotten by the Hindus, and condemn worldly pursuit, impurity, pride, and repetition of anything other than God’s name.

l: Guru, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Guru is a spiritual guide and Giver who gives God's name, explains the Word, teaches truth, and provides divine knowledge. It is figured as ladder, boat, raft, lake, sea, sacred stream, house of snow, and lamp of the three worlds: a means of crossing the ocean of the world, meeting God, becoming pure, and reaching God's abode and court. Kind and merciful, the true Guru reveals and shows God, opens understanding, gives the true Name and God's instruction, and enables recognition of God's will and the Bridegroom. Its instruction dispels doubt, ignorance, fear, suffering, pride, worldly love, demerits, and misery; settles arguments; purifies heart and mind; and protects those seeking salvation. Service, thought of the true Guru, and the Guru's favour bring peace, devotion, divine meditation, knowledge, freedom from entanglements, release from transmigration, and union of humanity with God. The account moves from the Guru's broad saving metaphors and gifts, through its teaching and transformative effects, to instruction concerning salvation and preservation. It closes with a warning that a person without a guru has no virtues and against people who merely call themselves gurus and beg.

l: the Name, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: God's name is presented as a true, pure, unfailing wealth: nectar, jewel, merchandise, capital, support, and object of meditation. It has infinite sweetness and value, sustains man, brings honour, purity, wisdom, devotion, contentment, peace, happiness, and access to God's court. Remembering, repeating, adoring, treasuring in the heart, and reverencing the Name, especially under the True Guru's instruction, remove sin, fear, pride, greed, doubt, sorrow, pain, disease, mourning, separation, worldly desire, worldly love, error, transmigration, rebirth, hell, and Death's net. It frees and delivers human beings, enables crossing the world, causes meeting and absorption with God, protects the soul, assists at the Last Hour, and is necessary for salvation. The Name is superior to religious ceremonies, ablutions, alms, offerings, calls to prayer, the horn of the Jogi, and other religious acts; without it, learning, dress, austerities, cleverness, and practices are vain and lead to suffering. It is to be thought of, heard, spoken of, and repeated, including on the tenth lunar day. Its culminating claim is that it is the highest and only unfailing religious act, containing six religious duties; however, selling it by writing it is condemned.

l: the Word, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The Word is true, the Word of the true Guru, and the highest spiritual discourse: a means of devotion, meditation, and attention wherever one sits. It dwells in the heart, manifests God, moistens and awakens the heart when it has light, restrains the wandering mind, and extinguishes hopes, desires, and pride. Received through the Guru's instruction, accepted as true, taught to the heart, understood, and continually meditated upon, it gives divine knowledge, truth, love, honour, peace, happiness, service, and absorption in God. It cleanses heart and body, removes demerits and doubt, regenerates those who humbly follow it, and implants God's name in the heart. Those imbued or tinctured with it are delivered, united with God, become perfect Bairagis, obtain God's abode and the ambrosial fruit, and cross the terrible ocean into the True One's court. Religious acts, purifications, austerities, devotion, penance, and pilgrimages abide in it. The Word is also contrasted with those who reject it, lack it, or speak and write without fear of God: they wander, are punished on the road of death, or are watched by the god of death. Thus it begins as inner cleansing and discipline, unfolds through Guru-given understanding and devotion, and culminates in salvation, freedom from bondage and transmigration, and union with God.

l: God's court, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: God's court is an unrivalled true palace of honour, happiness, judgment, truth, and acceptance, containing three engraved destinies. False, impure, and God-separated people are denied entrance; those imbued with God's Name and the Word, carrying true merchandise and following the Guru's instruction, receive honour and emancipation's robe.

l: woman, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: A woman is portrayed as a young bride and wife whose whole life is directed toward God as her Spouse and Beloved. Separated from Him, she is dishonoured, sleepless, impatient, and unable to find satisfaction in worldly ornaments, food, or pleasures. She seeks the love of the one God, belongs to Him exclusively, and offers her soul and body to Him. Through the Guru’s word, God’s Name, truthfulness, obedience, and love, she becomes dyed with God’s Name, absorbs herself in God, and experiences happiness, divine companionship, and peace. Her heart, body, and soul are fulfilled by God; she possesses nectar-filled tanks and ambrosial fruit in her own home. Her conduct matters: falsehood and lack of merit cause her Spouse to forget her, while pleasing Him brings honour. The account moves from longing separation to meeting and union with the Bridegroom through God’s favour, culminating in lasting honour, happiness, and peace.

l: man, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Man is a mortal, perishable trader in the world, with a body of blood, semen, wind, water, and fire, and a soul, breath, and body belonging to God. Created, sustained, and sheltered by God, he is born according to the heart’s desires and is subject from the beginning to destiny, death, and God’s account. His life is brief and uncertain; when its measure is full, death summons him, examines his accounts, and his actions bring their own reward and fruit. Worldly possessions cannot accompany him. Man’s central danger is forgetfulness of God. Attachment, passion, greed, pride, falsehood, pleasure, status, ritual, possessions, and varied phases and directions of life lead him astray. He forsakes ambrosia for poison, accumulates demerits, becomes entangled, and, without the Guru or God’s Name, suffers wandering and transmigration after an unprofitable death. Religious garb, pilgrimage, and austerity do not bring comfort without the Name. The records urge man to subdue pride, adopt virtues, practise truth, serve God and the true Guru, meditate on and repeat God’s Name, and love the True One. Through God’s favour, the Name, the Guru’s instruction, service, virtue, and becoming the holy man’s slave, he obtains happiness, honour, salvation, emancipation, and rescue. Humanity is also taught that God’s light is in every heart and all people are equal.

l: the Qazi, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The Qazi is condemned for falsehood, lies, and eating filth; a true Qazi, through the Guru’s favour, turns men from the world and is dead while alive.

l: Pandits, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Pandits read the Veds and claim this dispels sinful inclinations, but without understanding, delight in the Word, and love of God's Name, their reading is secular and ends in disgrace.

l: mammon, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Mammon is the evil, beloved worldly attachment to wealth, desire, and possessions. Spread as a net, it bewitches and deludes humanity, drawing the mind in every direction. It produces covetousness, greed, pride, superstition, false or counterfeit conduct, anxiety, unhappiness, and forgetfulness of the Name; it ruins the virtuous woman separated from her Spouse and absorbs one whose heart is filthy and hard. Those who make it their friend cannot recognize the real treasure within, obtain the water of life, or reach God's mansion. Attached people wander in the ocean of the world, face Death's gate and transmigration, and finally die and blend with dust. Its attraction is ultimately exposed, set aside, and must be abandoned with its entanglements.

l: truth, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Truth is presented as superior to every other practice and as the central way to please God, recognize God, enter God’s court, obtain honour, and reach the True One. It is bestowed by God, learned through the Guru and the true Name, and obtained by practising it. Truth purifies a person, serves as acceptable ablution for a body defiled by falsehood, and makes one true when held in the heart. It requires abandoning falsehood, greed, pride, and sin; false pride is condemned. Truth also appears as fasting and modest spiritual conduct, and it ultimately prevails when falsehood ends.

l: virtue, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Virtue brings happiness, purity, knowledge of God, and union with the Perfect One; it is required for happiness and leads to God when embraced. It abides with the person who embraces it, drives vice away, and cuts off chains. Good works are necessary for heaven, salvation, honour, and freedom from punishment, unlike sin, hypocrisy, and empty observances. Virtue unfolds as a tree: God's name forms branches, religion flowers, divine knowledge fruit, attainment of God leaves, and mental pride dense shade.

l: God's love, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: God's love unites people with God, brings the soul home to the True One, and leads toward emancipation. It matters because it fulfills the heart's desire, preserves honour with God, removes pride, and makes people fearless, peaceful, and detached from worldly desires. It is likened to the lotus, fish, chatrik, water, chakwi, and sun in longing and protection. Those dyed with it pray to God, exchange hearts with Him, and are not separated from their Spouse. True love preserves honour; without it, love becomes hate, and ritual that forgets the Beloved is condemned. It is a jewel filling the heart, an ornament of the virtuous woman, and food for the few on the right spiritual way.

l: pride, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Pride is an inner force that makes the heart impure, sustains worldly attachment, blocks spiritual understanding, and causes false claims, suffering, transmigration, and subjection to death. It arises from beauty, wealth, status, and religious display, affecting kings and religious figures as well as others. Worldly offerings do not remove it. Under the Guru’s instruction, meditation on God’s Name and the Guru’s Word dispel or remove pride, bringing genuineness and supreme dignity. It is ultimately to be forgotten, subdued, and made to depart through the Word.

l: Death, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Death is the universal force that ends embodied life, separating body and soul and reducing the body to dust. It overtakes every person regardless of learning, rank, wealth, ritual, family, authority, or possessions, and it destroys bodies, kings, wealth, and created beings. It acts as a tax-gatherer, binding people according to deeds, punishing sin with its mace, noose, agents, and difficult road. The deceitful and those attached to mammon are led captive to Death’s gate, where regret, blows, and transmigration follow. Those ignorant, attached to worldly desire, lacking the Word, forgetting God, or failing to repeat God’s praises face fear and punishment. Yet Death cannot espy a person whose heart holds God’s true Name. Remembering and praising God’s Name, receiving God’s favour, and following the Guru’s teaching defeat Death and protect the person from its tortures.

l: the ocean of the world, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The ocean of the world is fearful, dangerous, boundless, and boatless. Its coming and going is deceptive and impermanent; possessions, rulers, cities, pleasures, and beings cannot endure. The holy cross it through God's name, and the true Guru ferries those favoured by the Guru.

l: the intoxicant illusion, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The intoxicant illusion gives man temporary pleasure, causing forgetfulness of death, while contrasting with abstainers’ truth and God’s name’s lasting intoxication.

l: the boat, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is a means of crossing [the ocean of the world] The boat represents the means of crossing toward God and is identified with the Guru. The Guru is also called the ladder, raft, lake, sea, and sacred stream that carry man across the ocean of the world.

l: the counterfeit, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The counterfeit encompasses false merchandise, conduct, devotion, and hypocrisy; it lacks caste and honour, is rejected by God, and brings transmigration.

l: wealth, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Wealth, including possessions and authority, is impermanent, robs the world, and entangles people; it ends at death, while God's name is pure wealth.

l: the body, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The body is an impure, temporary mixture of wind, water, and fire, with nine gates and a tenth door and soul within the heart. It is called a carriage, palace, temple, and house of God, yet depends on breath, is burdened by worldly conduct, and finally falls into dust or ashes, leaving possessions behind.

l: the soul, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The soul is an immortal, conscious being dwelling within the heart and originating from a strange land. At bodily death it leaves the body and departs the world, yet does not die when spiritual ignorance ends. Separated from God, it suffers and becomes entangled in death through pride, mammon, counterfeit conduct, and worldly attachment. The Guru, the Word, and God's name bring understanding, satisfaction, and deliverance.

l: the heart, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The heart contains God and God’s eternal light, yet without God’s essence and the Word it is impure, changeful, unstable, and burdened by pride, worldly love, desire, lust, and greed. Through the Guru’s instruction, favour, and meditation on the Name, it becomes fixed and pure, gains divine knowledge, happiness, truth, nectar, freedom from disease, and extinguished burning.

l: the mind, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The mind is impure, restless, distracted by worldly occupations, and attached to worldly love, wandering under greed, deceit, pride, mammon, and false understanding. Through the Guru’s instruction and Word, it recognizes the world as a dream, is restrained and purified, fixed on God, penetrated by God's name, and gains peace and happiness.

l: religious ritual, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_inferior_to God's name [even in great quantity] Religious ritual, including penance, austerities, pilgrimage, alms, repeated ceremonies, prayer, reading, and bodily suffering, is insufficient without God, truth, and God's name. The text teaches that ritual without the Guru and the Word cannot remove sin, pride, or transmigration.

l: the Veds, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The Veds are read by Pandits, but reading alone neither destroys sinful inclinations nor dispels ignorance without understanding.

l: Ghar III, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Ghar III teaches how Sat Sangat and Duhagins are known. It says that those pleased with God's will remove superstition from their minds and that Nanak, the true Guru, is known by his association with every one.

l: Sat Sangat, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Sat Sangat is the Society of the holy, known through mention of the name of the one God.

l: God's will, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Those who are pleased with God's will remove superstition from their minds.

l: Sri Rag ki War, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Sri Rag ki War teaches that faith and resignation characterize the holy, while patience is the viaticum of angels. It says that all creatures have one shelter, that of God, and that divine favor can change how creatures are regarded.

l: the Perfect One, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The Perfect One is obtained through uttering and singing true praise, bringing satisfaction and comfort under the Guru's instruction.

l: the fool, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The fool mistakes possessions and pleasures for lasting goods, enters disputes, cannot learn from instruction, and is said to require being smitten on the mouth for friendship.

l: human life, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Human life is a fleeting mansion of smoke, unfolding through attachment, desire, household concerns, aging, weakness, and death; its lasting value lies in remembering God and following the Guru.

l: house, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: A house welcomes friends and Spouse, becoming bright and joyful with saints; empty without love’s sweets or the Bridegroom’s delights.

l: sin, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Sin defiles man inwardly through sinful pleasure, though it seems sweet briefly before its fruit turns bitter. It arises when people neglect truth, virtue, self-restraint, and the Name while pretending goodness, and it brings chains and punishment at Death's gate. Outward washing cannot erase it; humility, God's Name, and the Guru's instruction wash it away, ending it when the true Guru unites man with God.

l: the True Guru's instruction, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The True Guru's instruction is a path of spiritual teaching and discipline. It calls people to remember the Name, recognize God's will and presence in every heart, speak truth, and practise contentment, charity, and service. It rejects greed, pride, falsehood, worldly love, superstition, and evil inclinations, restraining the mind and giving divine understanding. It adjusts the soul's affairs, reveals God's court at home, brings protection and happiness, and culminates in salvation, emancipation, freedom from transmigration, and absorption in the True One.

l: caste, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: has no power [the reality is tested instead] Caste has no power in determining spiritual reality. What matters is obedience to God's order, which makes a person noble in God's court.

l: obedience to God's orders, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a steed [sent into the world by the Master] Obedience to God's orders is sent into the world like a steed, while reflection on the Guru's instruction serves as its kettle-drums. Some people prepare for this journey and others set out upon it.

l: greed, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Greed is a heart-burning worldly entanglement that causes the false to miss God's palace until the Guru's instruction quenches it.

l: wrath, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Wrath, a destructive stream joining lust and love for woman, assails, plunders, and ruins human beings and sinners.

l: worldly love, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Worldly love is a destructive stream of fire and worldly sin that binds people to desires, family, possessions, wealth, and sensual pleasures. It intoxicates the mind, creates anxiety, error, transmigration, and the pain of birth and death, causing people to forget God’s Name and waste human life. It begins in attachment and pursuit, deepens into entanglement and suffering, and departs through God’s favour, the Guru’s instruction, the Guru's Word, and God's Name.

l: the Guru's tree of contentment, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The Guru's tree of contentment blossoms in religion, fruits divine knowledge, grows through good works and meditation, and brings honour and the greatest gift.

l: the minstrel, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The minstrel, once out of work, is appointed by God to sing God’s praises night and day, summoned to God’s true court, clothed in true praise, and given ambrosial food of the true Name.

l: fear of God, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Fear of God is necessary for salvation and love; it adorns humanity, fashions the Word, and destroys fear of transmigration and empty understanding.

l: Gauri Ashtapadi, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a composition [a section of Rag Gauri] Gauri Ashtapadi teaches that clothing, luxury, beauty, power, wealth, titles, and supernatural claims cannot bring happiness without God’s Name. It praises Guru’s instruction, humility, truth, and devotion as the means of knowing God.

l: Gauri Chhant, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a composition [a section of Rag Gauri] Gauri Chhant portrays the bride’s painful longing for her absent Beloved and her joy when united with Him. It teaches that the Name, truth, contentment, Guru’s instruction, and God’s favor bring union, peace, and fulfillment.

l: the pious, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The pious are holy people associated with the Name through spiritual fellowship, truth, divine knowledge, and God’s love. They worship God, thirst for truth, and are freed from filth, pride, and worldly entanglement through God’s praises. Carrying on true dealings according to God’s will, they escape Death’s noose and punishment. Absorbed in the True One, they are known in God’s court, invited to God’s palace, and blended with God.

l: lust, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: ruins human being [with wrath] Lust is a worldly desire that ruins sinners when joined with wrath and draws human beings away from the Real Thing. Those absorbed in lust fail to recognize God’s essence.

l: God, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: God is the Creator, primal and infinite True Being, cause of causes, emperor and Lord. God creates and sustains humanity and the universe, pervades everything and all three worlds, fills sea, land, and lower regions, and is present as light in every heart. God is eternal, unborn, self-existent, ever young, beyond death and destiny, without caste, form, colour, or outline; unseen, imperceptible, inaccessible, omnipotent, and boundless. God holds creatures’ ways in hand, arranges human affairs, knows virtues and secrets, directs acts, judges the world by deeds, sends and recalls people, and may pardon them. God is also the Giver, Benefactor, Merciful One, True Cherisher, and lover of all: protecting people and lower animals, bearing their anxiety, giving wisdom, truth, knowledge, peace, happiness, greatness, forgiveness, contentment, the Name, and salvation. God gives favour, leads people to the True Guru’s instruction according to former actions, removes suffering and ignorance, and blends those who love the Name with the True One. Without the Guru, God causes transmigration; through love, God grants salvation. God is not pleased by obstinate penance or many religious garbs, but requires love and service. As Beloved and Spouse, God comes home to the bride through the Guru’s instruction and divine favour. Union with the bride brings joy, peace, praise, fulfillment, companionship, and exchanged hearts. God delights in, favours, visits, and is loved by the devoted young woman. Those who live in God’s attributes and knowledge day and night, fix their minds firmly on the True One, and love the jewel of the Name are blended with God in every age.

l: Rag Asa, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a spiritual composition Rag Asa teaches that God alone creates, sustains, judges, and grants truth. It urges man to abandon worldly attachment, empty ritual, pride, and reliance on status, and to seek God through the Guru, devotion, and the true Name.

l: Asa Ashtapadi, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a spiritual composition Asa Ashtapadi teaches that the Word and God’s Name bring peace, freedom from sin, protection from death, and union with God. It condemns worldly attachment, greed, pride, false learning, and religious display, and commends service to the Guru and meditation on the Name.

l: saints, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Saints bring happiness and brightness to homes; meeting them brings rejoicing, divine knowledge, and spiritual fulfillment.

l: Brahman, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The Brahman is condemned for taking life then bathing; true Brahmanhood reflects upon God, saving oneself and all relations.

l: Sanyasi, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Sanyasi is a renunciant who serves Guru, remembers and loves the one God’s Name, subdues passions, and is satisfied; hypocrisy instead brings dress, begging, hoarding, and ignorance.

l: Jogi, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Jogi unfolds from ignorance of union with God and ruinous influence to true knowledge of God and recognition of the One through the Guru's favour.

l: Jogis, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Jogis are portrayed critically as ascetics who beg, wear ashes and patched coats, yet may remain hypocritical and attached to wives. Without the Word and the true Guru, their twelve sects, halters, and breath-control lead to ruin. A Jogi who receives the Guru's instruction, meditates, accepts alms of love, and sees all equally instead dwells peacefully.

l: world, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The world is God’s created and sustained place of temporary existence, pervaded by God but filled with sin, mammon, entanglement, and desire for sweetness over bitterness. People live in it briefly, hearing and speaking of God, yet often forget the Creator, trade like transient shopkeepers, amass wealth despite death, and become intoxicated with worldly love. It is ruined by the ignorant Jogi, lying Qazi, and life-taking Brahman. Its condition unfolds through images of a frail cord that soon snaps, a terrible ocean of wandering and suffering, and transient lightning and fire. Empire, wealth, beauty, nobility, and youth rob it, while people face judgment for deeds. The Guru’s instruction, dispelling doubts, frees people from entanglements and enables them to cross the ocean; God’s name cools its fire.

l: devotion, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Devotion is a penance and purification of the heart that requires the Name and good acts. It unfolds through remembering and praising God, serving and accepting the Guru, and practising truth, contentment, mercy, and faith, cleansing the heart and leading through the world’s dangerous ocean to God’s favour and salvation.

l: contentment, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Contentment is described as a place of pilgrimage, made by those foremost in God's favour and pure water for the Brahman.

l: salvation, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Salvation is obtained through God’s Name, the Guru’s instruction and guidance, devotion, love of God, good works, and truth, not outward religious acts alone. It frees people from worldly entanglements, sin, transmigration, fear, and death, bringing them into God’s presence.

l: transmigration, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Transmigration is a disease and state of repeated birth and death, suffered when humanity or man forgets God’s Name, goes astray, and remains in spiritual ignorance. It is linked with darkness, doubt, worldly attachment, sin, evil actions, mammon, and ignorance of the Word, including the effects of good and evil acts across life’s phases. It unfolds as repeated existence until release comes through service to the True Guru, the Guru’s instruction and favour, divine knowledge, humility, God’s love and favouring glance, remembrance and repetition of the Name, and union or absorption in God.

l: religious ceremonies, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Religious ceremonies are entanglements tied to hopes and desires when done without devotion and understanding. Without meditation or knowledge of God, they are worthless, empty, or vain, and are inferior to God’s Name. Purifications, austerities, pilgrimages, ablutions, and decorations are rejected unless they lead to God; repetition of the Name is the exception.

l: true merchandise, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: God's Name is true merchandise and unfailing spiritual wealth. Repeated with the tongue and remembered, it destroys sin, gives wisdom, knowledge, and understanding, profits humanity day and night, and cools the world's fire. Those who traffic in it gain profit, preserve their capital, receive honour and tranquilly meditate on God. Unlike worldly wealth, it accompanies people after death, brings God’s favour, and leads to freedom, happiness, and God's court.

l: happiness, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Happiness comes to a God-favoured wife and one devoted to the Beloved, received through God's name when God orders, with love and divine companionship.

l: divine knowledge, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Divine knowledge is a rare, peaceful treasure recognized by one who inquires of and thinks of the true Guru. Obtained through favourable destiny and the Guru, it makes a person a servant of the True One, dispels mental ignorance, and reveals God’s form through spiritual sight. It is likened to salve for beholding God and material for an enduring lamp of devotion; it brings the benefit of pilgrimage through immortal water. It is necessary for emancipation: outward practices, religious display, learned texts, and appearances cannot reveal the Real Thing without it. Pure knowledge guides understanding, worship, honour, and alms, while wisdom used for wrangling is not true wisdom.

l: Rag Gujari, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a hymn Rag Gujari teaches that the heart should be cleansed through the Name, good acts, and meditation on God. It says that ritual without the Name is futile, that God is near and caring, and that devotion leads toward purity and deliverance.

l: Gujari Ashtapadi, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a ashtapadi Gujari Ashtapadi consists of prayers for love of God's pure Name and teachings on God's service, the true Guru, the Word, and freedom from worldly suffering. It says that repeating God's name and following the Guru's instruction bring divine knowledge, peace, stability, and release from transmigration.

l: God's service, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: God's service is required for happiness and gained through the true Guru's favour; through loving service, prayer, repeating God's name, and good works, a person crosses the ocean of the world.

l: death, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Death ends every person’s worldly existence at God’s appointed call, bringing separation, misery, and judgment for deeds; wealth, family, status, and possessions do not accompany anyone. Its pain ends when the true Guru unites man with God and he beholds the Spouse.

l: Bihagre ki War, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Bihagre ki War says that the Hindus have forgotten God and are going the wrong way. It describes their worship of stones and questions how a sinking stone could carry them across.

l: Hindus, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Hindus forget God and go the wrong way, following Narad’s instruction. Described as blind, dumb, ignorant, foolish, and immersed in superstition, they worship stones and consider ablution of the Chandal and foul.

l: Rag Wadhans, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a religious composition Rag Wadhans presents the fervent woman's longing for God and the Beloved. She decorates herself but is not accepted, mourns separation, seeks to see God in dreams, and offers her head and life in service.

l: Wadhans Chhant, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a religious composition Wadhans Chhant teaches that truth in the heart is the acceptable ablution and that God's word and name bring happiness. It says that God grants human life according to past acts, that people should avoid quarrels and jealousy, and that God's name is greater than alms and good works.

l: Wadhans Alahanian, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a religious composition Wadhans Alahanian says that God created the world and drew it within Himself. God is present in every heart and is known through the Guru's instruction and meditation on the Name.

l: Wadhans ki War, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a religious composition Wadhans ki War declares that ritual should perish when it causes a person to forget the Beloved. It identifies true love as that which preserves a person in honour with God.

l: fervent woman, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: A fervent woman, enamoured of God’s glances, longs for the Beloved and weeps in separation. Unaccepted despite adornment and needing no worldly ornaments, she offers her head and life as sacrifice and service to God.

l: destiny, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Destiny is a condition for favourable understanding and governs all creatures from the beginning. It is written on each forehead and engraved in God's court; what is destined takes place and will be obtained. The foolish do not read its lines. God alone is not subject to destiny and executes His order.

l: Rag Sorath, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a religious composition Rag Sorath teaches that all must die and part, that those who forget God suffer, and that God alone is the Benefactor. It praises God's greatness and urges humanity to repeat God's Name, serve the Guru, and seek protection so the soul may blend with the Supreme Soul.

l: Sorath Ashtapadi, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a religious composition Sorath Ashtapadi teaches resistance to mammon, rejection of empty rituals, and devotion to God through the Guru's instruction. It describes the Bairagi, the Pandit, destiny, and the power of God's Name to free humanity from doubt and transmigration.

l: Guru, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Guru is a dispenser of weal and woe, compared to a lake containing jewels, and a giver and procurer of emancipation. The True Guru is the source of the real boon and ambrosial Name. Through service, words, instruction, association with saints, and favour, Guru gives God's Name, love of God, divine knowledge, steadfastness, and God within. Guru breaks pride, doubt, fear, wandering, hypocrisy, and entanglements; protects man as the Fearless One; and makes people pure and worthy of honour at the true court. Those at the Guru's feet are led to the Beloved, God's court, freedom from transmigration, and union with God, away from error, sorrow, sin, and death.

l: Bairagis, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Bairagis are devotees defined not by outward identity but by abandoning desires, treasuring the Word, fearing God, serving the Guru, and loving God alone. They may remain at home or beg alms to fix love on God, becoming perfect, content with the Name, and absorbed in divine pleasure.

l: Pandit, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: recites religious scriptures [as a worldly affair] The Pandit is criticized for chattering about the Shastars and Veds while treating them as a worldly affair. The text teaches the Pandit that meditation on the Supreme Being, rather than hypocrisy or empty learning, is the religious practice that brings happiness.

l: Lord of the three worlds, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: has flavour [which the impure man does not obtain] The Lord of the world is the name that should be repeated.

l: Rag Dhanasari, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Rag Dhanasari is a rag containing Dhanasari Ashtapadi and Chhant, teaching devoted service, remembrance, destiny, accountability, and rejecting deceit.

l: Dhanasari Ashtapadi, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Dhanasari Ashtapadi teaches that God is satisfied by human love and service, not obstinate penance or religious garb. It says that remembrance of God's name leads to piety and absorption in God, while stone worship, pilgrimage, forest dwelling, and renunciation do not purify a filthy mind.

l: Dhanasari Chhant, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Dhanasari Chhant says that a woman who pleases her Spouse is honoured in His house. A woman who utters falsehood is not regarded by her Spouse and suffers painful nights.

l: thief, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The thief is a counterfeit person whose praise or reviling cannot affect the magistrate; nobody guarantees him. Regardless of dress or ingenuity, he receives his actions’ fruit and is known by God.

l: Musalman, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Musalman is one who cleanses impurity and requires a guru or priest for acceptance.

l: Spouse, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: does_not_look_at woman [when she utters falsehood] The Spouse honours a woman who pleases Him but does not look at one who utters falsehood.

l: Rag Suhi, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Rag Suhi teaches that man should not forsake ambrosia for poison or remain bound by worldly entanglements. It praises service to the True One and says that recognizing oneself as neither good nor bad brings salvation.

l: Suhi Ashtapadi, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Suhi Ashtapadi describes the soul as a bride lacking beauty, merit, wisdom, and good conduct, yet capable of pleasing the Spouse through divine knowledge, humility, and devotion. It teaches that attachment to mammon causes loss, while love of the True One prevents rebirth and leads to union with the Beloved.

l: Suhi Chhant, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Suhi Chhant celebrates the arrival of the Spouse and the saints, whose presence brings happiness, nectar, divine knowledge, and the jewel of love. It teaches that the Guru removes the soul's misery and that longing, love, and remembrance lead the mind home to the True One.

l: Suhi ki War, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Suhi ki War teaches that God tests the genuine and counterfeit in the divine court and condemns hypocrisy, falsehood, empty ritual, and irreligious company. It praises the Name and God's praises above ritual calls, Vedic reading without understanding, and outward cleansing.

l: meditation, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: provides alms of love [under the Guru's instruction] Meditation on the Name, the Word, and the Guru's instruction supports devotion and salvation. The Jogi who receives the alms of contemplation can overcome worldly pain.

l: water, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Water is pure, generates the world, quenches thirst but cannot wash the heart, and finally destroys everything.

l: Rag Bilawal, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a religious hymn Rag Bilawal presents Nanak's praise and devotion to God. It describes Nanak's humility, his inability to comprehend or describe God fully, and his efforts to make his heart a temple and avoid being born again.

l: men, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Men are depicted as dishonourable and dishonest, consuming carrion, speaking falsehood, and gaining an evil reputation after death. Yet the human body and heart can house divine realization. Humanity is warned against vice and attachment, but may find freedom through recognizing the True One, the Guru’s instruction, and God within.

l: the tenth day of the lunar month, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: calls_for_repetition_of Name [as offerings and ablutions] The tenth day of the lunar month is a time to repeat the Name as offerings and ablutions.

l: meditation, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Meditation on the True One is presented as pure ablution, a cooking square made by few, and a proper spiritual practice centered on God.

l: impurity, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Impurity does not cling to the heart when doubts and fears have fled, and is absent in songs, knowledge, moon, sun, corn, ablution, rain, earth, water, and air; it is associated with the mouth of one who turns away from God.

l: Ramkali, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a religious composition Ramkali presents teachings on devotion to God, the Name, meditation, good works, and the Guru's instruction. It describes the dangers of mammon, pride, worldly love, sin, and hypocrisy, and teaches that salvation comes through devotion and remembrance.

l: Ramkali ki War I, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a religious composition Ramkali ki War I criticizes religious hypocrisy among Gurus, Qazis, Brahmans, Musalmans, Jogis, and others. It teaches that truth, good works, remembrance of the Name, and service to God matter more than outward practices.

l: emancipation, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: depends_on serving the Guru Emancipation cannot be obtained without the true Guru and devotion to the primal God. The Guru grants and procures it, while love of God, truthful living, and the Name lead people to it.

l: Rag Maru Ashtapadi, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a religious composition It teaches that hypocritical Sanyasis, householders, Jogis, and Kaparis who lack the Guru's instruction remain attached to greed, lust, pride, and superstition. It praises the true Sanyasi who serves the True Guru, subdues the passions with God's Name, and fixes attention on God's feet.

l: Maru Solhe, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a religious composition It teaches that God is inaccessible and unfathomable, but is found through the true Guru's instruction, devotion, and remembrance of the Name. It describes the consequences of false dealings, attachment to mammon, and forgetting God, and praises those who pursue truth and carry on true traffic.

l: Maru ki War I, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a religious composition It teaches that creation occurs by God's order and that God will call people to account for their love, conduct, and state of heart. It says that pride, doubt, fear, and transmigration depart through the Guru's wisdom and remembrance of God's Name.

l: God, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: God is the one, inaccessible and unfathomable, without father, mother, son, or brother. God creates, sustains, carefully supports, and pervades the world, three worlds, humanity, and every heart; God is life within all lives. Dwelling in the human heart, God gives nectar, wisdom, knowledge, understanding, happiness, and merciful emancipation. God knows hearts, speaks through wind, water, and fire, decides human fate, and judges in God's court. God is known through meeting the true Guru, receiving instruction in the heart, devotion, and continual remembrance of the Name, which cools the world's fire and rejoices the heart.

l: apostate, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The apostate forgets the Name, follows error and evil passions, and suffers pain, bondage, and transmigration because he does not know the Guru's word.

l: religious life, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_preserved_in home [by drinking God's essence] Religious life is presented as service to the Guru, remembrance of God's Name, humility, truthful conduct, and control of the passions. External dress, pilgrimage, silence, begging, and learned disputation do not constitute true religious life without love of God and the Word.

l: Bhairo, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Bhairo teaches that offerings, penance, worship, learning, pilgrimage, religious dress, and bodily austerities are of no avail without God's name.

l: Rag Basant, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a great month Rag Basant praises the month in which spring begins and urges remembrance of the Sustainer of the earth, meditation on God, and the adoption of excellent virtues.

l: attainment of God, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: Attainment of God is described as the fruit in the metaphor of good acts as a tree.

l: Sarang ki War, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a war Sarang ki War presents teachings about purity, wisdom, worship, truth, and right conduct. It condemns idol worship, dishonest religious behavior, and empty religious practices.

l: idol, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: An idol kept in a house with attendant gods receives washing, worship, kungu, sandal, and flowers, yet gives no sustenance or preservation from death.

l: right way, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: The right way is recognized through honest labour and embodies truth, contentment, divine knowledge, meditation, mercy, forgiveness, good deeds, and God's love.

l: Rag Malar, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a hymn Rag Malar teaches that people should shun covetousness, pride, evil inclinations, slander, lust, and wrath. It says that wisdom, knowledge, understanding, and lasting profit come from God's name, while love of God comes through association with the saints and instruction from the Guru.

l: Malar Ashtapadi, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a hymn Malar Ashtapadi portrays intense longing for the Beloved through the chakwi, lotus, chatrik, fish, and separated woman. It teaches that the Beloved is present within all, and that through the Guru's favour people find God in their hearts and become absorbed in Him.

l: Malar ki War, Hymns of Guru Nanak
s: is_a hymn Malar ki War teaches that prayers, worldly status, wealth, beauty, nobility, and youth cannot prevent death or bondage.
